value.overview: The Barn Swallow is a widespread, graceful swallow recognized by its deeply forked tail, blue-black upperparts, and warm reddish throat and forehead. It breeds across much of the Northern Hemisphere and spends the nonbreeding season in tropical and southern regions. It is strongly associated with open landscapes and human structures, where it often nests on buildings. Its long, pointed wings and agile flight help it catch flying insects over fields, wetlands, roads, and settlements.
value.classification: The Barn Swallow belongs to the swallow family Hirundinidae and the genus Hirundo. It is one of several closely related red-throated swallows found across the world.
value.identification: Adults have glossy blue-black upperparts, a reddish-brown forehead and throat, and pale underparts that may be washed with buff. The throat is usually separated from the breast by a dark band. The tail is long and deeply forked, with small white spots visible on the outer tail feathers. In flight, the species appears slim and long-winged. Juveniles are duller, with shorter tail streamers and less strongly colored throat markings.
value.rangeHabitat: The Barn Swallow has one of the broadest breeding ranges of any swallow, occurring across North America, Europe, Asia, and parts of North Africa. It winters mainly in Central and South America, Africa, southern Asia, and northern Australia. In Costa Rica it occurs primarily as a nonbreeding migrant, with birds present during the northern winter; some individuals may also pass through during migration. It uses open country, agricultural areas, wetlands, pasture, river valleys, towns, and other landscapes with abundant flying insects.
value.migrationStatus: Migratory in Costa Rica. Birds from northern breeding populations arrive mainly during the nonbreeding season, generally from late year into the first part of the following year, and depart northward in spring. Timing and abundance vary by location and weather.
value.breeding: Barn Swallows usually breed in sheltered sites on buildings, bridges, barns, caves, and similar structures. The nest is an open cup made largely of mud and lined with grass, hair, and other soft material. Both adults commonly participate in nest construction and feeding. They may raise more than one brood where the breeding season is long. Costa Rica is not generally considered a major breeding area for the northern migratory population, although local breeding records should be interpreted by region and subspecies.
value.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on flying insects, including flies, beetles, wasps, bees, and flying ants. It usually captures prey in open air while flying low or at moderate height over fields, water, roads, and livestock areas. Barn Swallows may drink by skimming over water and often forage near grazing animals, which disturb insects. Feeding activity is generally greatest in warm, calm conditions when insects are abundant.
value.behavior: Barn Swallows are highly agile fliers that make rapid turns, climbs, and swoops while pursuing insects. They often perch on wires, fences, branches, or building edges between feeding flights. Outside the breeding season they may gather in large roosts, especially in reed beds or dense vegetation. In Costa Rica, migrants may be seen singly or in groups over open habitats, wetlands, agricultural land, and settlements.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although the species remains widespread and abundant overall.
